拍子木發出清脆、明亮的撞擊聲，具有乾淨俐落的質感。其音色尖銳而富有穿透力，音域集: The hyoshigi gives a crisp, bright knock with a clean, decisive quality. Its timbre is sharp and carries well, concentrated in the high frequencies, with no sustain: it is a short percussion sound. Because it is two pieces of hardwood or bamboo, the material itself resonates little and the sound comes mainly from the two striking each other. Compared with warm, rounded bells and chimes, the hyoshigi is harder; compared with drums its sound is thinner and has less depth. This distinctive clack marks time very strongly and cuts cleanly through the musical texture; it is often used to emphasise rhythmic points and mark the joins between sections, and in Japanese traditional music it plays an important part in leading the rhythm.
拍子木起源於中國，後傳入日本並逐漸演變成具有日本特色的樂器。在日本傳統藝能中，拍: The hyoshigi originated in China, later reached Japan and gradually became an instrument with a Japanese character. In Japanese traditional performing arts it came into wide use in the Edo period, becoming an important accompaniment tool in kabuki, joruri and other stage forms. This simple, ancient instrument consists of two pieces of hardwood or bamboo, usually joined by a decorative cord; the player makes a crisp sound by knocking the pieces together or striking them on the floor.
拍子木（Hyoshigi）屬體鳴樂器，發聲體為兩片硬木或竹，通常以細繩連接。來源: The hyoshigi is an idiophone whose sounding element is two pieces of hardwood or bamboo, usually joined by a thin cord. The source does not state the material of any other part, nor whether there is any resonator or decorative fitting. It does not sound by way of a reed or a membrane but by solid bodies striking each other; it is played by clapping the two pieces together or striking them on the ground, which gives the knock.
拍子木（Hyōshigi）是日本傳統體鳴樂器，屬拍板類，由兩片硬木或竹以細繩連接: The hyoshigi is a traditional Japanese idiophone of the clapper type, made of two pieces of hardwood or bamboo joined by a thin cord. It is played by clapping the pieces together or against the floor, and the pace can start slow and get faster. It is used in kabuki, bunraku and other theatres to announce the start of a performance, and kyogen players use it to open a comedy; theatre, sports and acrobatics directors can use it to draw the audience's attention. At festivals it is used to direct the mikoshi, and it plays with traditional instruments in the mikagura-uta (song cycle) of Tenrikyo.

The hyoshigi is not only used to beat time; its particular sound also heightens the tension and expressiveness of a performance. As Japanese traditional performing arts have spread around the world, this old instrument's influence has reached the international stage, and it has become one of the symbols of Japanese culture.
